sop-from-memo.output:
WATER HEATER SWAP

YOU WILL NEED
Water main shutoff valve · breaker panel · garden hose · floor drain · new water heater unit · new flex connector lines · faucet on closest fixture to heater · camera or phone for photo · van toolkit

STEPS

1. Shut the water at the main valve — do not rely on the tank's isolation valve alone. Listen for water flow to stop completely.

2. Kill the breaker to the heater at the panel. Verify power is off by testing a nearby outlet or light switch.

3. Connect the garden hose from the van to the tank drain and run it to the floor drain. Open the drain valve fully and let the tank empty completely — this takes 10-15 minutes typically.

4. Disconnect the cold inlet and hot outlet lines from the old heater using your wrench set.

5. Remove the old heater from its location and position the new unit in place.

6. Install new flex connector lines on both cold inlet and hot outlet — use new lines every time, even if old lines appear intact.

7. Fill the new tank by turning the main water valve back on. Listen and feel the lines — they will be cold and then warm as water flows.

8. Bleed air from the system by opening the faucet closest to the heater (usually a sink in the same room or adjacent room). Run it for 30 seconds until water flows smoothly with no sputtering.

9. Turn the breaker back on. Wait 2 minutes for the heater to stabilize.

10. Wait 20 minutes, then inspect all connections, the tank base, and flex lines for any drips or pooling water.

11. Take a photo of the installed heater and new lines for the job file.

DONE LOOKS LIKE
No water flowing from any drain or connection. Heater powered on and heating. Faucet runs clear without air bubbles. All flex lines are dry after 20 minutes. Photo is filed.

COMMON MISTAKES & HOW TO CHECK

Forgetting the expansion tank or not accounting for a check valve on the main — if the customer has a check valve and no expansion tank installed, pressure will build and you will see slow leaks or a hiss at the relief valve within hours of startup. Ask the owner before you start whether a check valve is on the main line, and if so, confirm the expansion tank is present. Mark it in the photo.

Powering on before the tank is full and air is bled — the heating element runs dry and fails. Check: run the closest faucet for 30 seconds and feel the line temperature rise smoothly before you flip the breaker.

Checking for leaks too soon (at 2 minutes instead of 20) — small seals need time to seat. Set a phone timer for 20 minutes and walk away. At 20 minutes, inspect again with a dry rag so you spot even a bead of moisture.
